description: First published in English in 1959, this book revolutionized contemporary thinking about science and knowledge and is one of the most widely read books about science written in the twentieth century. It presents succinctly Popper's view of science and his solutions to two fundamental problems of the theory of knowledge: the demarcation of science from non-science, and the role of induction in the growth of scientific knowledge
Originally published: New York : Basic Books, 1959

docs.creator: Karl Popper
docs.description: Karl Popper’s The Logic of Scientific Discovery (first published in German in 1934 as Logik der Forschung, and in English in 1959) is arguably the most important text in the 20th-century philosophy of science. The book completely upended the prevailing view of how science works. Before Popper, the standard view (championed by the Logical Positivists) was that science progressed through induction—gathering evidence to prove a theory true. Popper argued the exact opposite: science progresses by attempting to disprove its own theories. Here is a breakdown of the foundational arguments in the text. 1. The Rejection of Induction Popper begins by attacking the "Problem of Induction" (a concept dating back to David Hume). Inductive reasoning assumes that because we have observed a phenomenon happen many times, it will always happen. Popper argued that no number of supporting observations can definitively prove a universal law. His famous example is the white swan: no matter how many thousands of white swans you observe, you cannot logically conclude that "all swans are white." However, the observation of just one black swan definitively proves the statement false. Therefore, scientific laws are logically incapable of being completely verified, but they can be completely falsified. 2. The Demarcation Problem Popper wanted to draw a clear line between genuine science (like Einstein’s theory of relativity) and pseudoscience or non-science (which, for Popper, included astrology, Freudian psychoanalysis, and Marxist history). He called this the Demarcation Problem. His solution was the Criterion of Falsifiability. A theory is only scientifically valid if it is theoretically possible to prove it wrong. Good Science: Makes bold, risky predictions. (e.g., Einstein predicted light would bend around the sun during an eclipse. If it hadn't, his theory would have been destroyed.) Pseudoscience: Explains everything and predicts nothing specific. It twists itself to accommodate any new piece of contradictory evidence, making it unfalsifiable. 3. Conjectures and Refutations Because we cannot prove theories true, Popper proposed a deductive scientific method based on trial and error: Conjecture: Scientists propose bold, imaginative hypotheses to explain a problem. Refutation: Scientists then rigorously test these hypotheses, actively trying to tear them down and find flaws. Science does not survive by sheltering its theories, but by throwing them into the fire. The theories that are currently accepted in science are simply the ones that have not yet been falsified. 4. Corroboration vs. Truth Popper replaces the concept of "scientific certainty" with "corroboration." When a theory survives rigorous testing, it is not "true"—it is merely highly corroborated. In Popper’s framework, all scientific knowledge is provisional. We are never completely sure we have found the absolute truth; we just have theories that are progressively less wrong than the ones that came before them. Science is an endless quest for truth, but one where absolute certainty is impossible.
